cards.question: Suggest where to add measurements if a thermometric graph has too few points near its maximum.
cards.answer: Add points around the expected maximum or intersection while retaining coverage on both sides.

cards.question: Describe choosing observation times in a thermal reaction.
cards.answer: Measure a stable pre-mixing baseline; sample frequently during the rise; continue into cooling so a transient maximum is not missed.

cards.question: Suggest why waiting several minutes for a stable final temperature can underestimate an exothermic rise.
cards.answer: Heat can leave the mixture before that reading, so the transient maximum has passed.

cards.question: Describe selecting repeats for a titre mean.
cards.answer: Exclude the rough run; find careful titres within0.10 cm³; mark the closest suitable pair and average them while retaining the other recorded trials.

cards.question: Suggest what to do with an unexpectedly high careful titre.
cards.answer: Retain and investigate it, then repeat the run to check for overshoot or another cause rather than silently deleting it.

cards.question: Describe confirming CO2 after effervescence in a specified carbonate test.
cards.answer: Collect or direct a suitable gas sample under the supervised method; pass it into limewater; record a milky appearance as confirmation supporting CO2.

cards.question: Suggest the supplied confirmatory test for ammonia evolved on warming with alkali.
cards.answer: Damp red litmus turns blue in the gas; record the observation under the instructed procedure.

cards.question: Describe selecting a reagent to distinguish Al3+ and Zn2+ using supplied notes.
cards.answer: Recognise both NaOH precipitates dissolve in excess; test fresh portions with aqueous ammonia; Al precipitate remains in excess whereas Zn precipitate dissolves.

cards.question: Suggest a follow-up for a white barium-nitrate precipitate when sulfate and sulfite are the candidates.
cards.answer: Apply the supplied nitric-acid follow-up: sulfate precipitate remains while sulfite precipitate dissolves.

cards.question: Describe a coherent raw-and-derived titration table.
cards.answer: Include trial identifiers/rough label; align initial and final readings with titres; put units in headings and mark the careful values selected for the mean.

cards.question: Calculate the two titres and their mean for trials with initial/final readings0.20/24.85 and0.10/24.80 cm³; retain the rows in a results table.
cards.answer:
|Trial|Initial / cm³|Final / cm³|Titre / cm³|
|---|---:|---:|---:|
|1|0.20|24.85|24.65|
|2|0.10|24.80|24.70|
Equation/working: titre=final−initial; mean=(24.65+24.70)/2=24.675 cm³, about24.68 cm³ to two decimal places. The values differ by0.05 cm³ and are concordant; retain unrounded mean in later calculations.

cards.question: Describe preparing a gas-volume experiment table before the run.
cards.answer: Read the planned intervals; draw Time / s and Gas volume / cm³ headings; leave enough rows for the full range, repeats and any endpoint note.

cards.question: Calculate the missing titre in a prepared table row with initial reading1.10 cm³ and final25.75 cm³. Show the completed row headings.
cards.answer:
|Initial reading / cm³|Final reading / cm³|Titre / cm³|
|---:|---:|---:|
|1.10|25.75|24.65|
Equation/working:25.75−1.10=24.65 cm³. Answer retains0.01 cm³ decimal places; the raw readings follow0.05 cm³ increments.

cards.question: Describe separating raw, calculated and conclusion columns in a mass-loss experiment.
cards.answer: Keep initial/final masses as raw readings; calculate their difference in a labelled mass-loss column; record the chemical inference separately with its supporting method.

cards.question: Calculate and enter mass loss from raw masses52.64 and52.20 g in a table with separate raw and derived columns.
cards.answer:
|Initial mass / g|Final mass / g|Mass loss / g|
|---:|---:|---:|
|52.64|52.20|0.44|
Equation/working:52.64−52.20=0.44 g, answer to the raw hundredth-gram place. Gas escape is a separate inference, not a raw balance reading.

cards.question: Describe correct headings when time and reciprocal time are both tabulated.
cards.answer: Name Time / s and1/time / s−1 separately; define symbols if ambiguous; put reciprocal values under their reciprocal unit rather than under seconds.

cards.question: Calculate reciprocal times for100.0 and50.0 s and provide the derived column heading.
cards.answer: Equation:r=1/time. Working:1/100.0=0.01000 and1/50.0=0.0200; answer heading1/time / s−1. Values are0.01000 and0.0200 s−1 with significant figures reflecting each supplied time.

cards.question: Describe consistent raw reading and qualitative recording.
cards.answer: Use decimal places supported by the instrument throughout each raw column; preserve trailing zeros; give comparable colour, solid and excess-behaviour detail across samples.

cards.question: Calculate the mass difference from2.85 g and2.40 g on a0.01 g-resolution balance and state recording precision.
cards.answer: Equation: difference=final−initial. Working:2.85−2.40=0.45 g. Answer keeps the hundredth-gram place; raw2.40 must retain its trailing zero. Significant figures do not override raw scale resolution.

cards.question: Describe the calculation chain for unknown HCl concentration from a NaOH titre.
cards.answer: Convert titre cm³ to dm³; use n=cV and the balanced1:1 mole ratio; divide HCl amount by aliquot volume in dm³ and report justified precision.

cards.question: Calculate HCl concentration if25.00 cm³ acid is neutralised by24.675 cm³ of0.100 mol dm−3 NaOH.
cards.answer: Equation:HCl+NaOH→NaCl+H2O; n=cV. Working:Vbase=0.024675 dm³; n=0.100×0.024675=0.0024675 mol. Answer:cacid=0.0024675/0.02500=0.0987 mol dm−3 to three significant figures. Retain unrounded intermediate amount.

cards.question: Describe choosing significant figures for a calculated result.
cards.answer: Identify the least accurate measured input; retain guard digits through working; round the final result to matching precision or one extra significant figure where justified by the syllabus convention.

cards.question: Calculate a product mass from0.0500 mol and molar mass58.0 g mol−1, stating justified precision.
cards.answer: Equation:m=nM. Working:0.0500×58.0=2.90 g. Answer has three significant figures matching the inputs; quantities already use mol and g mol−1 so no conversion is required.

cards.question: Determine a suitable display for sample-by-sample precipitate colour and excess-solubility results.
cards.answer: A labelled qualitative results table, with separate initial and excess observations.

cards.question: Suggest a display that reveals how gas-production rate changes during one run.
cards.answer: Plot gas volume against time and retain the raw table; the curve gradient shows changing rate.

cards.question: Determine which quantity belongs on the vertical axis for gas volume plotted against time.
cards.answer: Gas volume / cm³; time / s is horizontal.

cards.question: Suggest a readable horizontal scale for times0–100 s across five equal major intervals.
cards.answer: 20 s per major interval, giving a0–100 s range.

cards.question: Determine the correct horizontal position of25 s on a scale with marked20 and30 s.
cards.answer: Halfway between20 and30 s.

cards.question: Suggest how to retain a genuinely anomalous plotted value while excluding it from a fit.
cards.answer: Ring or label the point and explain its exclusion; keep the original table reading.

cards.question: Determine whether a straight line or a smooth curve fits a gas-volume response whose gradient steadily declines.
cards.answer: A smooth curve showing the declining gradient.

cards.question: Suggest why joining noisy successive points with sharp corners can misrepresent a smooth reaction trend.
cards.answer: The corners can turn random scatter into artificial changes in the underlying rate.

cards.question: Determine a suitable vertical variable to test proportional endpoint-rate behaviour when each run reaches the same small endpoint.
cards.answer: 1/time / s−1, a fixed-endpoint rate proxy, plotted against concentration.

cards.question: Suggest the key endpoint requirement for comparing rates using1/time.
cards.answer: Each run must reach the same defined extent or endpoint under matched other settings.

cards.question: Determine the meaning of the intercept4 cm³ in V=0.400t+4 with t in s.
cards.answer: The model predicts a volume4 cm³ at zero time; its physical cause depends on the experimental baseline.

cards.question: Suggest how to reduce coordinate-reading influence when calculating a straight-line gradient.
cards.answer: Use two well-separated coordinates on the fitted line and a large gradient triangle.

cards.question: Determine whether the tangent or a whole-run secant gives the local rate at40 s on a curved volume–time graph.
cards.answer: The tangent gradient at40 s.

cards.question: Suggest the physical meaning of area under a volume-production-rate versus time graph.
cards.answer: Accumulated produced volume over the interval, because(cm³ s−1)×s gives cm³.

cards.question:
Determine the rate trend shown by the gas-volume graph over0–40 s and40–80 s, using supporting volumes.

Original model V=60(1-exp(-t/40)). Tangent at40s has gradient0.5518 cm3/s; time range0 to100s, volume0 to65cm3. Curve not experimental data.
cards.answer: The graph rises from0 to about37.9 cm³ by40 s and then to about51.9 cm³ by80 s. Smaller gain in the second equal interval supports a declining average rate.

cards.question: Suggest two numerical features that distinguish faster reaction from greater final gas amount.
cards.answer: Compare an early gradient for rate and the plateau volume for final amount; they describe different features.

cards.question: Determine the useful distinguishing observation if both candidates form white NaOH precipitates soluble in excess but only one dissolves in excess ammonia.
cards.answer: The excess-ammonia solubility difference, recorded on fresh portions.

cards.question: Suggest how to improve a summary recorded merely as “tubeA white, tubeB clear”.
cards.answer: State whetherA contained a precipitate and whetherB was a colourless solution, then add each change with excess reagent.

cards.question:
Determine the unknown concentration by reading the calibration graph at its indicated signal0.70.

Signal dimensionless versus concentration mol/dm3. Straight model S=20c+0.1 over0.01 to0.05; marked measured standards. Horizontal guide at signal0.70 crosses at concentration0.03. Read the unknown from the graph.
cards.answer: The horizontal signal0.70 guide meets the fitted line at concentration about0.030 mol dm−3. Read the corresponding x-coordinate; this is interpolation within the measured range.

cards.question: Suggest how to check an unknown estimate lying beyond the measured calibration range.
cards.answer: Measure additional suitable standards nearer the unknown; compare their fit before relying on extrapolation.

cards.question: Determine which titres to average from a rough25.30 cm³ and careful24.65,24.70,25.10 cm³ runs.
cards.answer: The careful24.65 and24.70 cm³ pair; exclude rough and investigate25.10.

cards.question: Suggest why a mean without individual repeats can hide a problem.
cards.answer: Averages can conceal large scatter or an anomalous run, so preserve the component values and selection reason.

cards.question: Determine the sign of the gradient on a measured mass–time graph that decreases with time.
cards.answer: Negative; its magnitude can represent mass-loss rate if that convention is stated.

cards.question: Suggest why very close tangent coordinates give a less reliable gradient.
cards.answer: Their small differences make coordinate-reading uncertainty a larger fraction of the slope calculation; choose a larger triangle.

cards.question: Determine whether temperature is controlled if starting values rise20.0,22.0,25.0°C as concentration increases.
cards.answer: No; temperature changes systematically with concentration and can affect the measured rate.

cards.question: Suggest a temperature control and a check for a concentration-rate experiment.
cards.answer: Equilibrate mixtures in a thermostatic bath and record starting liquid temperatures to verify comparability.

cards.question: Determine the likely direction of heat-loss error on an exothermic enthalpy magnitude calculated from solution warming alone.
cards.answer: It lowers the observed rise and underestimates the exothermic magnitude.

cards.question: Suggest an improvement targeting an observed gas leak rather than scale resolution.
cards.answer: Reseal/check the joints and tubing before repeating; a finer scale would not recover escaped gas.

cards.question: Determine the simple maximum uncertainty in a titre obtained from two burette readings each ±0.05 cm³.
cards.answer: ±0.10 cm³, adding the two absolute reading uncertainties.

cards.question: Suggest why measuring a larger temperature rise can reduce percentage reading uncertainty when each temperature has unchanged uncertainty.
cards.answer: The absolute uncertainty in the difference stays similar while the measured rise increases, reducing the uncertainty-to-rise ratio; keep the changed reaction amount accounted for.

cards.question: Determine the error type if repeated readings scatter unpredictably above and below a central value.
cards.answer: Random error.

cards.question: Suggest why repeating a calorimetry run without changing a persistent heat-loss mechanism cannot remove its bias.
cards.answer: The same systematic loss remains in each repeat; insulation or a suitable correction addresses the cause.

cards.question: Determine the supported ion among Al3+ and Zn2+ if a white precipitate dissolves in excess NaOH but remains in excess ammonia.
cards.answer: Al3+, from the supplied candidate outcomes.

cards.question: Suggest how to qualify a conclusion from two results whose difference is smaller than their plausible uncertainty.
cards.answer: State that the data do not clearly resolve a difference and obtain more precise evidence before claiming a change.

cards.question: Determine whether a rising1/time–concentration line with a clearly nonzero intercept establishes direct proportionality.
cards.answer: No; exact proportionality requires an intercept consistent with zero within the relevant uncertainty.

cards.question: Suggest how to test a prediction at a concentration outside the original measured range.
cards.answer: Run controlled repeats at new suitable concentrations and compare the resulting endpoint rates with the extrapolated model.

cards.question: Determine an explanation for a declining gas-volume gradient as a reacting solution is consumed.
cards.answer: Reactant depletion can reduce successful collision frequency and hence rate, under the stated reaction setting.

cards.question: Suggest why an observed temperature rise does not by itself give an exact reaction enthalpy.
cards.answer: The calculation also needs amount, heat capacity/mass assumptions and consideration of heat transferred to the vessel/surroundings.

cards.question: Determine the targeted improvement for variable manual delay at a timed endpoint: a bath or automated timing trigger.
cards.answer: An appropriate automated timing/endpoint trigger targets that delay; a bath addresses temperature instead.

cards.question: Suggest a specific calorimetry improvement and explain the error it reduces.
cards.answer: Use an insulated vessel with a lid to reduce heat exchange with surroundings, improving the measured temperature rise.

cards.question: Determine which is an extension to a concentration-rate study: repeating the same run or investigating temperature at fixed concentration.
cards.answer: Investigating temperature at fixed concentration answers a new question and is an extension.

cards.question: Suggest a controlled extension asking whether solid particle size changes rate.
cards.answer: Use equal masses of the same solid in defined size fractions with fixed solution concentration/volume/temperature; measure the same endpoint and repeat each fraction to compare rate.
